name: Hexoprenaline
lead: Hexoprenaline is a selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist used as a bronchodilator for asthma and, in some countries, as a tocolytic to relax the uterus, with Gynipral the most commonly cited brand [1]. It is a prescription medicine and is not approved by the US FDA [1].

It belongs to the same pharmacological class as beta-2 agonists such as clenbuterol and salbutamol, which is the reason it is filed alongside fat-loss compounds in this wiki's catalogue. No source documents hexoprenaline itself being used for fat loss or physique, and its published use is clinical.
Research on hexoprenaline covers asthma, preterm labour, external cephalic version and obstetric procedures [2][3][4].

angle.text: Hexoprenaline is a beta-2 agonist, a class whose better-known members are discussed for fat loss. Hexoprenaline's documented use is medical, in asthma and obstetrics, and no community use for appearance is recorded.

infobox: Rx-only; Schedule 4 in Australia; not FDA-approved

paras: Hexoprenaline is used for asthma, and in countries such as Russia and Switzerland to suppress labour [1]. An early report introduced it as a new bronchodilator in 1972 [5]. A 1977 controlled trial in 20 asthmatic patients found oral hexoprenaline reduced the fall in peak flow after exercise in 16 of them compared with placebo [6].

Betamimetics as a group reduced the number of women giving birth within 48 hours in a Cochrane review of trials in preterm labour [7]. Hexoprenaline has been compared with ritodrine for tocolysis before external cephalic version, with atosiban in preterm labour, and has been tested to relax the uterus during suprapubic amniocentesis [8][9][10][11].

Oral bioavailability is roughly 5 to 11 percent, peak levels occur around 2 hours and the oral half-life is about 50 minutes [1]. Hexoprenaline is not metabolised by MAO or COMT in the way isoproterenol is [12]. Beta blockers reduce its effect, and caffeine and theophylline can increase it [1].

Contraindications for tocolytic use include hyperthyroidism, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, shock and placental abruption, with caution in gestational diabetes; combination with some anaesthetics or other adrenergic agonists can cause arrhythmia [1].

Randomised and controlled trials have examined hexoprenaline in asthma, tocolysis for preterm labour and external cephalic version, and obstetric procedures [6][8][9][10][11]. No studies of hexoprenaline for fat loss or body composition were found.

timeline.event: Described as a new bronchodilator in a South African medical journal report [5].
Controlled trial of oral hexoprenaline in exercise-induced asthma in Australia [6].

card.summary: A beta-2 agonist medicine for asthma and labour suppression, in the same class as fat-loss stimulants like clenbuterol.
card.note: Prescription-only; cardiovascular effects possible; not FDA-approved.

quick.overview:
Hexoprenaline is a prescription beta-2 agonist used for asthma and, in some countries, to suppress preterm labour.

It shares a drug class with clenbuterol, which is discussed for fat loss, but its documented use is clinical.
quick.mechanism: It activates beta-2 receptors, relaxing airway and uterine smooth muscle.
quick.risks: Prescription-only, not FDA-approved. Cardiovascular effects such as arrhythmia are noted, and several conditions contraindicate its use in pregnancy.
